q: UNIX was developed at which organisation, starting in 1969?
explain: UNIX development began in 1969 at AT&T Bell Laboratories. Berkeley later produced BSD.

q: Who were the principal developers of UNIX?
explain: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie developed UNIX at Bell Labs.

q: The first implementation of UNIX ran on which machine?
explain: UNIX first ran on a DEC PDP-7 minicomputer.

q: In which language was much of UNIX rewritten in 1973 to make it easier to port?
explain: Early UNIX used assembly language; rewriting it largely in C made it portable across hardware.

q: The early name UNICS is commonly expanded as:
options: Universal Network Interface and Control System
explain: UNICS, commonly expanded as Uniplexed Information and Computing Service, later became UNIX.

q: Which UNIX feature means CPU time is shared among several tasks and users?
explain: Time-sharing divides CPU time among tasks and users, supporting multitasking and multi-user use.

q: CUI in the context of UNIX stands for:
explain: CLI is Command-Line Interface and CUI is Character User Interface - both are text-based.

q: In the UNIX hierarchical file system, the directory tree starts at:
explain: All directories form a tree rooted at /, the root directory.

q: Which UNIX component interprets user commands and starts programs?
explain: The shell is the command interpreter. The kernel is the core that manages resources.

q: In the four-layer view of UNIX, which layer sits directly above the hardware?
explain: The layers from bottom to top are hardware, kernel, shell, then utilities and applications.

q: How do programs request services from the UNIX kernel?
explain: Programs make system calls to ask the kernel for services; the kernel uses device drivers to talk to hardware.

q: Which of the following is NOT a responsibility of the UNIX kernel?
options: Designing the layout of application windows
explain: The kernel controls process scheduling, memory, devices and file-system services; it does not design application interfaces.

q: Which command is used to change file permissions in UNIX?
explain: chmod changes permissions, whereas chown changes ownership.

q: Permissions in UNIX are assigned to which three classes?
explain: Read, write and execute are the permission types; they are applied to the owner, the group and others.

q: What does execute (x) permission on a directory allow?
explain: On a file, x allows running it; on a directory it allows traversing the directory.

q: The principle "everything is a file" in UNIX means that:
options: Every system object is literally stored as a text file
Only text files can be stored on UNIX
Directories cannot exist separately from files
Many resources, including devices, use file-like interfaces
explain: It is a design principle - many resources have file-like interfaces - not a literal rule for every object.

q: BSD stands for:
explain: BSD originated at the University of California, Berkeley, and is informally called Berkeley UNIX.

q: Which text editor is associated with Berkeley's UNIX work?
explain: The vi editor and the C shell (csh) are associated with Berkeley UNIX.

q: Which of the following is NOT a BSD descendant?
explain: Solaris came from Sun Microsystems; FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD are open-source BSD descendants.

q: Which BSD descendant focuses on security and code correctness?
explain: OpenBSD is known for security and code correctness; NetBSD is known for portability.

q: AIX is a UNIX variant developed by which company?
explain: AIX (Advanced Interactive eXecutive) is IBM's UNIX.

q: Which UNIX variant was originally developed by Sun Microsystems?
explain: Solaris came from Sun Microsystems; Oracle acquired Sun in 2010.

q: Xenix was a historical UNIX variant from:
explain: Xenix was based on licensed UNIX and came from Microsoft. IRIX was from Silicon Graphics.

q: Which statement about Linux is correct?
options: It is a direct descendant of AT&T UNIX source code
It was developed by Sun Microsystems
It is a UNIX-like kernel developed independently, not from original UNIX source
explain: Linux is independently developed and UNIX-like; BSD systems are the ones with real UNIX ancestry.

q: GNU stands for:
explain: GNU is a recursive acronym: GNU's Not Unix. GNU/Linux is the Linux kernel plus GNU components.

q: Which of the following is NOT a UNIX system?
explain: Windows 11 belongs to the Windows NT family. macOS has BSD heritage and certified releases.

q: Which command opens the reference manual pages?
explain: man displays manual pages, for example man ls.

q: Which command pauses execution for a specified duration, such as "sleep 5"?
explain: sleep waits for the given time; uptime shows how long the system has been running.

q: Which command shows the username of the effective user ID?
explain: whoami shows the effective username; who lists current logins and last shows login history.

q: Which command lists the users who are currently logged in?
explain: who lists current login sessions; last shows recorded login sessions.

q: Which command is used to change an account password?
explain: passwd changes an account password, subject to permissions and policy.

q: Which command prints the path of the current working directory?
explain: pwd means print working directory.

q: The rmdir command can remove:
explain: rmdir removes an empty directory; removing files needs rm.

q: Which command is used to move or rename files?
explain: mv moves or renames; cp copies and rm removes.

q: Which command selects lines that match a given pattern?
explain: grep prints matching lines; cat only displays or joins file contents.

q: What does the pipe symbol | do in the UNIX shell?
options: Sends the output of the left command to the input of the right command
Copies a file into a directory
Adds execute permission for the owner
explain: A pipe connects standard output of the first command to standard input of the second.

q: Which command sends ICMP echo requests to test reachability of a host?
explain: ping tests reachability using ICMP echo requests.

q: Which statement about the kill command is correct?
options: It always forces an immediate stop of any process
It deletes the file of the program permanently
It sends a signal to a process, and the result depends on the signal
It shuts down the whole system
explain: kill commonly requests termination but does not always force a stop.

q: Which command shows network connections, routing or interface statistics?
explain: netstat reports connections and statistics; ifconfig displays or configures interfaces.
